fatal_errors: The as-deposited material is incorrectly assumed to be an ordered hexagonal, grain-boundary-rich crystalline phase; the target films and nanoribbons were amorphous or extremely finely disordered with only cubic-type short-range order.
The hypothesis imports the sharp first-order magnetostructural transition of bulk and ribbon precursors into the as-deposited films, where that transition was not observed.

It predicts transition broadening and reduced hysteresis rather than the observed annealing-induced increases in ferromagnetic alignment, magnetization, susceptibility, and modest peak entropy change.
No prior observations or cited evidence support the proposed grain-boundary stress mechanism.
explanation: The proposed inert, sub-recrystallization anneal partially resembles the 700 K treatment, and stress relaxation is one component of the target mechanism. The controlled annealed-versus-unannealed comparison, structural checks, stress measurements, and explicit falsification rule are reasonably discriminating. However, the hypothesis is built on the wrong baseline structure and magnetic process: the target material lacks the ordered hexagonal phase, conventional crystalline grain boundaries, and sharp first-order transition assumed here. In the target, annealing preserves the amorphous matrix while enabling short-range atomic reordering and relieving fabrication strain, reducing local pinning barriers and improving collective ferromagnetic alignment. The measured consequence was increased magnetization and a small increase in peak −ΔSM, not demonstrated broadening of a first-order transition. The answer also omits the relevant 700 K condition, 1 µm nanoribbon geometry, field range up to 50 kOe, broad 40–200 K response, low-temperature inverse effect, elastic-strain boundary, and spacing-dependent magnetic coupling.
